summary:
Nasarawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies across the country and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure on entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, states that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and confirms that the federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and to those involved with gay groups or organisations. It further warns that some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention.

Trans-specific violence is documented. BBC (9 August 2024) reports that the beaten body of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in the capital, in a suspected murder, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; an investigation was announced, and the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Despite formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

No source in the current inventory documents enforcement, arrests or facilities specific to Nasarawa State itself; the state-level picture is inherited from the national framework and from incidents recorded elsewhere in Nigeria.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
